routes.label: Factor first, then classify the two-digit divisors

question: How many positive two-digit integers are factors of \(2^{24}-1?\)
solution:
Factoring the large number reveals which prime factors a two-digit divisor can contain. Repeated difference of squares gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{24}-1
&=(2^{12}-1)(2^{12}+1)\\
&=63\cdot65\cdot4097\\
&=3^2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot17\cdot241.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(241\) is prime: none of \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), the primes below \(\sqrt{241}<16\), divides it.

A two-digit divisor cannot contain \(241\). It also cannot contain both \(13\) and \(17\), because \(13\cdot17=221>99\). This leaves three disjoint cases.

If the divisor contains neither \(13\) nor \(17\), it divides \(3^2\cdot5\cdot7=315\). The divisors of \(3^2\cdot5=45\) are \(1,3,5,9,15,45\). Using these either alone or multiplied by \(7\) gives precisely the two-digit values
\[
15,\ 21,\ 35,\ 45,\ 63,
\]
so this case contributes \(5\).

If the divisor contains \(13\), it is \(13\) times a divisor of \(315\) at most \(7\). Those possible cofactors are \(1,3,5,7\), giving
\[
13,\ 39,\ 65,\ 91.
\]
This contributes \(4\).

If it contains \(17\), its cofactor must be a divisor of \(315\) at most \(5\). The possibilities \(1,3,5\) give
\[
17,\ 51,\ 85,
\]
contributing \(3\).

Every two-digit divisor belongs to exactly one of these cases. Within each case, distinct cofactors give distinct divisors. Thus the total is
\[
5+4+3=\boxed{12},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
